messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: Triangle Diagnostics?
parts:
It would be nice to add these acceptance rate vs.
parameter value histograms into the posterior analysis
parts of Stan.

There are a couple of issues:

1. We're not currently recording proposed parameter
values that are not accepted. Given that the same idea
works across all of HMC, NUTS and NUTS II (should that
be "NUTS Jr."?) and even Metropolis, it shouldn't be
too hard to save it. We just need to produce some format
for it, because it shouldn't be written into the output
for real samples.

One possibility is to add it as a comment
to the CSV output the way the tuning parameter targets
are added. Another would be to create a separate
output file with a well-defined format for sampler
analysis (as opposed to sample analysis).

2. In general, aren't there going to be multivariate
interactions. The high rejection space for (alpha,beta)
may not be infomrative when projected down to one
dimension. (For example, a highly correlated bivariate
distribution with Metropolis.)

On 7/25/12 8:53 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> The 0.5 was just a random value that separated the two extreme cases (good tuning and bad tuning), so I'm happy to change it.
> But what do you mean by "the scale of the variable"?

Looking at this now, I might have been confusing the X axis
with probability of acceptance.

- Bob

Personally, I like the idea of a separate output file altogether.
That way if you switch this auxiliary output off you don't change the
format of the nominal output stats.

> 2. In general, aren't there going to be multivariate
> interactions. The high rejection space for (alpha,beta)
> may not be infomrative when projected down to one
> dimension. (For example, a highly correlated bivariate
> distribution with Metropolis.)

Yeah, it could be a problem (a more pathological example would be a 2D
triangle, i.e. a diamond). The univariate outputs won't indicate the
poor performing regions as easily (the regions of extreme accept
probability would be smeared out) but the information would still be
useful and a clever user could reconstruct the problem area.
